speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is seldom we advance very far in any parliament before we are reminded that, one by one, our ranks are certain to be thinned by the hand of death. Mr. D'Arcy Britton Plunkett, representative for Victoria, is the first member of the new parliament to have been taken from our midst. His death occurred only yesterday after an exceedingly brief illness, so brief in fact that many hon. members of the house were not aware of his indisposition until they read that he had passed away.
Mr. Plunkett was in his sixty-fifth year, and was unmarried. The circumstance that his death should have occurred in this city while he was attending to his parliamentary duties, that for this reason he should have been away from the many friends and associations of the constituency he represented, and that because of the seriousness of his illness it was impossible for any of his fellow members and associates in this city to have much in the way of contact with him in his last days, adds not a little to the feeling of sadness which we all experience at this time.
Mr. Plunkett entered parliament in a byelection in December, 1928. He was reelected at the general elections of 1930 and 1935. I shall leave it to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) to speak of his public services. To my right hon. friend Mr. Plunkett was not only a very loyal supporter but a very true personal friend. I hasten at once to express to him on behalf of the government and of all hon. members on this side, and also to hon. members of his party our feelings of very sincere sympathy with them in the loss they and
their party have sustained. May I say that the sense of personal loss which they experience will I am sure be shared in large measure by all who sat in previous parliaments with Mr. Plunkett, and also by others whose privilege it was to come to know him since the opening of the present parliament.
I should like on behalf of all hon. members to add a brief expression of sympathy with Mr. Plunkett's brothers and his nephews, who I understand, are his only immediate surviving relations and also a word of sympathy with the city of Victoria, which has lost its representative in this parliament.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the generous terms in which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has spoken will not soon be forgotten by those of us who knew Mr. Plunkett as friend and colleague. I should like on my own behalf as well as on behalf of those with whom I am associated to express to the right hon. gentleman, not as leader of a party but as leader of this house, our very sincere and grateful appreciation of his kind words on this occasion. '
We are once more reminded that death is ever with us. The sickle of the grim reaper has appeared very early in the life of this new parliament. Out of two hundred and forty-five members one has been taken from us, although it is now but May and we first met in February.
Mr. Plunkett came into the House of Commons in a by election in 1928. He was reelected in 1930, and in 1935 he was again reelected after a very strenuous contest. If one were to ask what qualities ensured his election in the city of Victoria I would say that essentially the first was that he was a man of integrity and of the highest character. He was not a man who wore his heart upon his sleeve, and many who did not know him little appreciated the kindly heart that beat under a somewhat, shall I say, rugged exterior. But those of us who came to know him realized not only that he was a man of character and integrity and of great simplicity and directness in speech and action, but that he was possessed of a sense of loyalty that nothing could destroy. He was proud of his city and proud to be the member for Victoria-prouder than most men who represent constituencies, because he had been absent in the great war for a very considerable time, and came back only to find confusion in his own business. When he was elected he felt it was indeed the proudest moment of his life. His pride in Victoria he expressed in many ways.
The Late D'Arcy B. Plunkett

As a public man he took but little part in the debates of the house, but he was most regular in his attendance both in the chamber and in committee, and made himself singularly well informed with respect to all matters which engaged the attention of pariiament. Over and above all that he was a man of great industry, although that fact may not have been apparent to those who sat in the chamber with him. He attended to his correspondence in a manner which I believe commended him to his constituents; he was always busy looking after the interests of his friends and constituents, whether they were his political supporters or otherwise.
He was a great Canadian in the sense that he believed in his country, its destiny and its future. Although he represented the city of Victoria, in the far west, he never forgot that in Ontario he had first seen the light. Obviously his loss to all of us is great, but even greater to those of us who knew him better than to others who knew him only casually. While in the first loss of a member of this parliament the house as a whole has suffered a bereavement that is not easily understood, we, small in numbers, who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, have lost a well beloved comrade and colleague and one who by his loyalty and devotion to those with whom he was associated and to his party had greatly endeared himself to all of us.
I never think of the passing of one who is active in public life and who has to endure all that public men must endure,-the vicissitudes of life, the vicissitudes of position, criticism, sometimes unreasoning, and commendation sometimes equally unreasoning -without recalling those beautiful words of Shelley. I believe upon this occasion I might well repeat them as indicating what must be the position of those who, in the midst of their public duties, are struck down and go to their reward:
He hath outsoared the shadow of the night;
Envy and calumny and hate and pain.
And that unrest which men miscall delight,
Can touch him not, and torture not again;
From the contagion of the world's slow stain.
He is secure, and now can never mourn
A heart grown cold, a head grown grey in vain.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has asked on one or two occasions if I would inform him and the house what legislation remains to be introduced.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO PROPOSED FURTHER LEGISLATION

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO PROPOSED FURTHER LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I thought so, it may be just as well to anticipate.
In addition to the bills and resolutions which appear under government orders and the budget resolutions which are to be found in the votes and proceedings of Friday last, there will be legislation based on the reports and recommendations of the several special committees-the committee on the Elections and Franchise Acts, the committee on pensions and returned soldier problems, the committee on the Canadian radio commission, the committee on the marketing of wheat and other grains, and possibly also of the committee on railways and shipping. How extensive this legislation may 'be it is of course, not possible to say until the committees themselves have reported.

Hudson Bay Route

The proposed additional legislation will include (a) bills respecting a national finance council, loan councils, based upon the amendment to the British North America Act, notice of which appears on the order paper in the name of the Minister of Justice; (b) amendments to the criminal code, including reference to section 98; (c) a bill respecting the national parks; (d) an amendment to the Customs Act; there may also be amendments to the Combines Act, the Post Office Act, the Relief Act, the Proprietary or Patent Medicines Act, the Dry Docks Subsidies Act, the Carriage of Goods By Water Act, and a bill respecting marketing. These will be for the most part minor amendments. Then possibly there may be supplementary estimates of limited amounts.
I wish to add this further reservation. I am giving to the house at the moment all that the government see as a possibility, but I should like to have the right reserved to introduce one or two other measures should this be found necessary between now and the time that parliament prorogues.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I would ask the permission of the house to proceed with a bill for interim supply with respect to the supplementary estimates which are now before the house. The bill provides for one-sixth of all the items in the special supplementary estimates, and an additional proportion, not exceeding one-half, of certain items. All of these calling for an additional amount are to cover payments falling due before the first of June on contracts which were made prior to April 1 or for payment of wages if the work was undertaken by day labour. There are a few exceptions to that statement to which I must refer.

Interim. Supply Bill
Relief for single, homeless men. The amount in the estimates covers the operation for three months only. Topographical and air surveys: A larger proportion is required in this case to equip and send out field parties as soon as possible. Of course provision is needed with respect to the general vote for grants in aid to the provinces to keep up with the monthly necessities in that regard. Another exception is with regard to the continuance of unemployment relief projects now organized which were covered by the special supplementaries for three months and which require to be spent regularly every month, and also to continue geological surveys.
If the house will be good enough to give unanimous consent, I should like to proceed. If that is impossible, this can stand as a notice of motion for to-morrow, but it would be more convenient to proceed with it to-day.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) spoke to me with reference to this matter before the house met and I intimated to him that so far as we were concerned there was no reason why he should not proceed at once. On the other hand, I should like to point out that by giving our consent to these appropriations we reserve our rights as though we had not given it, so far as the items are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It also raises a question of some seriousness, to which I directed attention the other day. We are giving our approval to the passing for the second time by this parliament of estimates dealing with items contained in the supplementary estimates as well as in the Public Works Construction Act, 1934, and the supplementary act of 1935. In this regard I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the statute requires that the Minister of Finance should file within thirty days of the opening of the house a report showing what expenditures have been made under the appropriations of 1934-35. I do not know for certain, but my memory is that such a report has not yet been filed. In the multiplicity of duties that fall upon the minister, I can quite understand why that has not been done. Subject to our right to discuss the items as though this consent were not given and without prejudice to our position with respect to the other point I mentioned the other evening and speaking only for those with whom I am associated, I see no reason why the minister should not proceed at once with his interim supply bill.

speechtext: I wish to thank my right hon. friend and to say by way of explanation that from the accounting point of view the expenditures which are now made and have been made under the authority of the Public Works Construction Act are being transferred to these appropriations as fast as possible. Naturally when that is completed and the authority for these estimates has been given by the house, it will be possible to repeal entirely the Public Works Construction Act. This is just a transition procedure but it does produce the situation to which my right hon. friend referred. I can assure the house that there certainly will not be double expenditures by virtue of proceeding in this manner.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Other projects-amount required for new works to be undertaken in cooperation with the provinces, $9,200,000-

Would the minister give a list of the projects by provinces?
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): I believe I pointed out previously that it was quite impossible to give a list of the projects to be undertaken under this vote. The reason lies in the fact that these projects are to be undertaken cooperatively with the provinces, and ;t is therefore necessary that we should negotiate with the provinces an agreement covering the work to be undertaken. Particular works to be covered by this vote will appear as a schedule to the agreement.
Are these amounts to cover expenditures made by the previous government?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: No, these are new works to be undertaken in conjunction with the provinces.
How did the minister arrive at the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It was difficult to arrive at an amount which would suffice for this purpose. Obviously it was impossible to provide public works in cooperation with the provinces sufficient to meet their respective employment requirements. We looked back over what had been done in recent years and- tried to strike, on the basis of what we felt was fair and reasonable in the circumstances, an estimate of what would be an adequate amount for such works during the forthcoming year.

Does the minister mean that he took the figures of the last few years and averaged them and decided on the amount on that basis?
Mr. ROGERS': This question was raised when the matter was before the house some days ago, and I suggested that this did appear
to be at least one method of approaching a sum which might meet the situation during the forthcoming year. Obviously it would be very difficult to get an exact estimate of what would be required or of what would be a reasonable amount to meet all the requirements of the coming fiscal year.

In other words, Mr. Chairman, I judge from what the minister says that he is putting in this blanket sum without having any particular idea of how much he will require. We come again to the same thing we discussed last sitting in connection with another item, that this is a sum which is more than he expects to require, but he has put in sufficient to cover all possibilities; in other words, he has put in as large an amount for this purpose as the previous government spent for these same objects under the so-called blank cheque. It amounts to this, that this is another way of avoiding what has been styled a blank cheque, at the same time keeping it entirely within the hands of the government as to how much they wilt spend for these purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I think there is this material difference between the two methods. Under the blank cheque legislation it might have been quite true that a sum of approximately ten million dollars was assigned during each succeeding year or upon an average during the last five years, but, as my right hon. friend understands, that was only a fraction of the total amount expended under the relief acts. Here we are restricting ourselves to a definite amount for public works to be undertaken in conjunction with the provinces, and elsewhere throughout these supplementary estimates we are setting definite amounts against specified items. My right hon. friend may object that the items are not sufficiently precise, but as I suggested some days ago, it is surely a misuse of language to say that this is a blank cheque in the sense in which that expression has been used during the last few years.
I think in fact this may have very much worse results than the blank cheque. The previous government under the authority given them spent some-think like this amount on an average-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Just on these works.

On these works. My opinion is that the minister is in a worse position with a fixed amount for these purposes than he would be under the legislation passed by the previous government. The reason I say that is that my experience taught me that when an amount is put in the

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
estimates for a particular thing, pressure is more effectively brought on the government to spend every dollar of that amount than it is under the so-called blank cheque legislation. If the minister will consult some of his colleagues I think he will find that when an estimate of $50,000 is put in for one department, the pressure is very great on the minister in charge of that department to spend the whole $50,000. Possibly when the estimate is made they think perhaps $30,000 or $35,000 may be sufficient, but they find it very difficult to keep the expenditure below the amount fixed in the estimate. The minister will find it almost impossible to resist the pressure to spend every dollar of this money. So long as there is any part of the estimate left how can he refuse an application from the provinces, and particularly from his friends in the different parts of Canada, to go on and spend money until it is all gone? In 1930 the previous government obtained from parliament a specific vote, I think it was $20,000,000, and I assure you that we found it easier under the legislation of the subsequent years, which has been called the blank cheque legislation, to resist applications for money for various purposes under the relief act than we did in 1930 when we had a specific sum appropriated for that purpose.
I do not propose to discuss the matter any further. I have already explained my view to the minister, and I know it was discussed the other evening when I was not present. I do not want to traverse the same ground aver and over, but I do feel that the present government are not putting themselves in any better position to resist unreasonable demands by this form of estimate than we were in under our legislation for the last four years.
Will a statement of the items be brought down before parliament prorogues?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: To the extent that agreements with the provinces are completed before parliament prorogues, we shall, I think, be in a position to place the agreements before the house. In the relief bill as originally drafted there was a specific provision for the approval of the agreements by resolution of the House of Commons, but exception was taken to the inclusion of that clause in the relief bill and it was deleted.

If no agreements are
reached with the provinces then we shall not know any more about these items than we know now. That is one objection we have; wre do not know that anything is to

be done; we do not know whether this amount will be spent. In regard to the blank cheque feature, for which the previous government were so much criticized, I always felt that the reason the blank cheque was asked for at the time was not to give the government unlimited scope but in order that they might restrict their expenditure. If we do not have the general items specified, is there any reason why this government should spend even the amount of the estimate? They may say that they did not come to agreements, and then nothing will be done. Again, we find the minister stating that the figures they have in the estimate now are arrived at from what the previous government did. Their criticism of the previous government was that it was not doing enough, was not dealing with the unemployment problem in a proper way. I have before me a newspaper report of one of the radio talks by the present Prime Minister during the general election, and one statement is, that "Bennett started too late to solve problem." If the present government are going to follow along the same line as the past government, what difference is the change of government going to make to the country?
I should like the minister to feel that we are not criticizing him just for the sake of criticism or in order to hear ourselves talk. He was rather annoyed on Thursday evening when there was some criticism from this corner of the house, but I should like him to feel that in no part of the house is he thought of more kindly than he is in this section. Not only in the house itself but in our group outside the house that is true. I have before me one of the papers that supports our movement, and in the notes from Saskatchewan I find this paragraph:	.
The Rosetown-Biggar M.P. had a few nice words to say of the Minister of Labour, Hon. Norman Rogers. The minister, said Mr. Cold well, was a man of vision and great ability, but was finding it very difficult to accomplish anything under the present order.
I also believe the minister has great ability, and it is because I want to continue in that belief that I suggest he try to get something done. On Thursday evening, looking at this section, he made this statement, as reported at page 2355 of Hansard:
I have no objection whatever to marching forward but I want to know where I am going. I want to know whether my next step is to be on firm ground or in quicksand, and I am not so sure that some hon. members are so anxious as to the direction in which they are going.
It is because we are anxious as to the direction in which we are going that we are criticizing. We are drifting; the minister cannot say where the next step is going to

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
be. No government can say where we are going so long as they leave the economic life of the country in the control of private individuals who exploit it for their own gain. It is to that we object. There is no reason why the government could not have a more specific program to place before parliament than that now before us. There has been plenty of time to produce it, although I have no doubt there are many things to do. Until we have some indication that something specific and ordered is going to be done we shall have occasion to complain, and I am afraid that under such circumstances the unemployed are not going to fare any better than they have fared in the past six years.

I think the minister might
give a little more information than we have had up to now. This item and others connected with it represent a program of works which the government offer for the alleviation of unemployment. Speaking in this chamber on Thursday evening last the Minister of Labour said the government were undertaking an expenditure of about $80,000,000 on a program for the relief of the unemployed. Is that statement correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I believe that covered all
expenditures in the various departments of government mentioned in the special supplementary estimates.

That is correct. I should like to have some break-down of these items, to know exactly what is being spent, not so much on public relief as on works to be undertaken to provide employment. In the expenditure of $80,000,000 works must be included which were started last year and are being completed this year. In it will be an amount the federal government will be giving to the provinces for relief purposes. At page 18 of the special supplementary estimates is found a summary, in which it is indicated that $30,418,341.66 is credited to projects already undertaken, and $28,430,401.76 to other projects. It is difficult for me, and I suppose for other hon. members, to ascertain how much of the first item remains to be spent in the present year. We may get an idea from the second item as to how much will be spent. I do feel that the minister is or ought to be in a position to inform the committee as to the amount of new works to be undertaken for the remainder of this year, and also the number of men the government expects will be able to find work as a result of expenditures undertaken in the supplementary estimates. I do not know whether the minister is in a position to give the committee that information, but if he is I certainly should like to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I regret that I am not in a position to give greater detail respecting expenditures than	is	set forth	in	thespecial supplementary estimates. The sum of $80,000,000. in round figures, to which I referred some days ago, was the sum which the hon. member has just described as being made up of sums	set	aside for	projectsalready undertaken but incompleted, and for other projects. Naturally I am under obligation in the supplementary estimates to deal with such items as come under the Department of Labour, but other ministers will deal with the estimates affecting their respective departments. That has been the procedure followed thus far,	and	it would	be	presumptuous on my part, for example, to deal with particular expenditures of the Department of Public Works, the Department of Marine or the Department of National Defence, except in so far as there may be some established connection between any of those departments and the Department of Labour. Relief camps would furnish an example of the kind I have indicated.The item before	the	committee	is	that
which deals with the .amount to be voted for works to be carried on in cooperation with the provinces. With no desire to withhold any information I must say we are not in a position to place details of these expenditures before the committee, owing to the fact that as yet we have not been authorized to negotiate agreements with the provinces for the construction of these joint works.
On former occasions we have emphasized that we were going to see that the dominion contribution to relief works so far as possible should be directed towards developmental activities. In other words we should have constantly in view some collateral employment or ultimate employment which might result through, let us say, the development of a mining area to which more satisfactory access has been afforded.
I regret to say I am not in a position to tell my hon. friend the amount of employment to be provided by these expenditures. I wish I had that information. I am bound to tell him and the committee that on the whole the results of employment under these relief works expenditures have been disappointing, in so far as their effect on relief rolls is concerned. I think we ought to understand that clearly, in order that we may not expect too great results from expenditures on relief works. I have no doubt the hon. member will have had information indicating the effect upon unemployment of large expenditures upon relief works in his own city of Winnipeg. I believe he will agree with me that the results of large expenditures on such works have been dis-

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
appointing, from the point of view of affording employment. All I can say is that we are giving very careful consideration to the feasibility of introducing into our agreements with the provinces clauses which will ensure that these relief works will have their due effect upon relief rolls. After all, we are approving the expenditures for that purpose, and I believe we are under obligation to see to it that in so far as the situation can be met in advance by means of explicit undertakings, we must arrange that these relief works shall provide at least a substantial quota of employment for those now in receipt of relief.

I am pleased to have received an answer from the minister. I expected something along the same lines. My reason for putting the question in a certain way was to ascertain what works were to be undertaken. When I put my question I had in mind the fact that during the past two years, when equivalent amounts were spent by previous governments to take care of unemployment in Canada, such expenditures provided for only a small fraction of the men who were out of work. I have in mind the Winnipeg situation. In that city two public buildings were erected. In addition a sewage scheme was undertaken, through cooperation of federal, provincial and municipal bodies. The expenditure of about SI,500,000 in the federal project did not touch the fringe of the problem. It is true that we have a couple of new buildings. They are ornate and possibly a first-class addition to the city of Winnipeg, but despite this great expenditure of money we have reverted to the situation which existed prior to the erection of the buildings. If this government is going to spend an average of the amounts spent by the previous government in the last five years, as the minister himself admitted, we will not bring about anything in the way of improvement in the unemployment situation. That is why many of us have suggested that the government adopt a broader and more fundamental policy in dealing with this problem. When this government took office it believed that what the previous government had done ' was totally inadequate, and hon. members in this part of the chamber were in complete agreement with that view.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? A few nights ago did he not acknowledge that the provisions of public works was in itself no solution for the problem of unemployment? Certainly I understood him to say that he did not favour large expenditures on public works.

No; I said that public works are not a solution for the unemployment [Mr. Bogers.1
problem, and by that statement I stand. They are not a solution. They are a palliative, and sometimes not even that. In many instances they tend to aggravate the situation because many public works which are undertaken become a burden to those who have control over them. I have in mind, for instance, the erection of barracks which are not needed. Some years ago in Winnipeg as a relief project a huge barracks was erected on the outskirts of the city at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars. I do not think a hundred people use it to-day. It is a huge building on the outskirts of the city, and although it cost a great deal it is of very little practical value, and is used by very few people. There are many such projects. I know public buildings that have been erected that are not in use to-day, such as a certain post office I have in mind. The Post Office Department did not know anything aJbout it; that is the information I have received. These buildings were put up and there they are to-day, almost unoccupied except for the caretaker. Projects of that kind cannot possibly help to solve the unemployment problem, and that is what I mean when I say that public works in themselves are no solution of the unemployment problem. They may give temporary help to men who have been out of work, and there is one thing we should bear in mind when dealing with people who have been out of work for months and months, some of them year in and year out: that there is nothing more demoralizing to the individual than that he should become continuously in receipt of relief. That is why it is desirable to have work made available as soon as possible, particularly for those who have been recipients of public relief for a number of years. Nine million dollars is totally inadequate for that purpose, because it can take care of only a very small fraction of the number of people who have been out of work in our large industrial areas in the past few years. The two projects in Winnipeg that I have named, the barracks and the post office building, did not take care of five or at the most ten per cent of the building trades mechanics who were out of work in the city, men who had been out of work for years and with very little hope of obtaining employment.
I would much rather see this amount of money spent on a class of work which will not only give useful employment but provide the community with something which is much needed and has been needed in this country for a number of years. I refer to a large scale federal housing scheme. I would

Supply-Labour-Reliej Works
rather see this amount and all these estimates used on a project of that kind than for. the erection of barracks and other buildings which have very little community value. The expenditure of twenty or thirty million dollars on a housing scheme in this dominion would give far more work than would be provided by certain types of public buildings that are to be erected under these estimates. Not only would it provide something that is immediately needed, but it would be a self-liquidating project, whereas the buildings to be erected under this vote are not. The people of this country need homes. It is one of the few things in the construction line that is needed, and that is why I am disappointed in the attitude of the government. I would much rather see them spend far more than the amount of all these estimates upon a comprehensive housing scheme for the dominion somewhat along the lines that have been followed in England and many other countries. That would set the wheels of industry turning again much faster than will the projects to be undertaken under these estimates. In Great Britain they have been building houses for the last fifteen years, and still they are not through building. In this country, from reports I have received, there is an acute shortage of houses in many of the larger industrial centres, and that acute shortage is having two effects. It is making the poor people double up in homes; it is resulting in an increase of rents. When people are unable to pay these rents it leads to overcrowding and to the many other problems that go with overcrowding. Public buildings do not provide even a partial solution of the unemployment problem, and that is why I urge the government so strongly to try new remedies which would be of more value under present economic conditions.

While I appreciate the impossibility of the minister specifying the exact projects to be undertaken, I would ask on what basis will agreements be made with the provinces. Will the cost be on a fifty-fifty basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The practice has varied
somewhat in past years as to the distribution of the financial responsibility. For works undertaken jointly by the dominion and the province the division of cost has usually been on a fifty-fifty basis, but in some cases the dominion has contributed forty per cent and the province sixty per cent. Where projects have been undertaken to which the municipality within the province has contributed, the dominion contribution has been proportionately less. All I can say at the moment
is that in working out these agreements with the provinces, where the proposed expenditures relate to highways, we shall be governed by what has been the well established practice under which the dominion contribution to a provincial highway shall not be in excess of fifty per cent of the total cost.

My real
object in asking the question was that I had information that similar projects carried out in different provinces received a different percentage of contribution from the federal government, one province receiving a greater percentage than another. Speaking for the province from which I come, I want to guard against any unfairness in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: In dealing with the provinces we shall seek to avoid any reasonable ground for complaint in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Exactly.
In the development of these expenditure schemes does the minister anticipate that in each case the initiative will be undertaken by the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes.

Then following up what the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) has said, I suggest that something be done to guarantee the interest on housing schemes undertaken by municipalities and cooperatively. If the capital is found for the purpose and the government is prepared to guarantee the interest, it seems to me that the revolving nature of the loan would enable these cooperatives to borrow at a very much lower rate than they can now when they have to pay both interest and capital. I think interest is the most distressing part of any business undertaking and sooner or later we will have to get away from it entirely and follow the teachings of Ruskin.

Mr. Chairman, I saw a May day parade in Toronto last Friday and if the minister had been there I am sure he would have been impressed with the magnitude of the task in front of him in providing employment for the unemployed of Canada. I do not wish to minimize the task he has before him; it really is colossal. In fact, I saw three different parades in Toronto, and if they are an indication of what this country is up against, this $9,000,000 is going to be

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
a mere bagatelle in taking eare of the people. As far as I can figure it out, this expenditure of $9,200,000, plus the expenditures by the provinces-I understand the provinces are to spend an equal amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Probably an equal amount; it is on a fifty-fifty basis.

That will make a total of $18,400,000. That should give direct employment to approximately 9,000 persons and indirect employment to an approximately equal number. This makes a total of about
18,000	to whom employment may be given, provided that materials do not use up too much of the vote. I quite agree that this is a substantial contribution, but it is nothing like what should be done to reduce the ranks of the unemployed.
I	was just wondering where the provinces are going to get the money. Ontario, Quebec and some of the other provinces may be able to obtain money on their bonds, but what about the provinces of which we have been hearing during this session? The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) has said that the province of British Columbia may be bankrupt, but that does not fit in with the statement in the paper this morning that that province is going to pay the interest on its bonds as well as the bonds which are due very shortly. The province of Alberta would appear to be bankrupt, and Saskatchewan does not seem to be very far behind. If the dominion must put up $9,000,000, plus another $9,000,000 in loans to the provinces, it is going to make it rather difficult for this government to carry on.
I want to support the minister in every possible way. I come from an industrial city with, including suburbs, about 800,000 inhabitants in which very many men and women have been unemployed for years. I wish the minister would come out boldly and announce some great big measures to provide more work. It seems to me that we are more or less playing with this problem. Ottawa is so far from the cushion, to use ordinary language, that it cannot get an accurate impression of conditions outside. After I am here a week I go away with a smile similar to those seen around Ottawa, but when I get back home I lose that smile very rapidly. There I am right up against the cushion and I know what the conditions are. The minister would have the support of this country if he grappled with this question in the largest possible way. This is not a question of politics; it is not a question over which this house should quibble about spending a few million dollars. During the election it was said that this

question would be grappled with in a big way, and I am sure the country will support
any measure the minister thinks necessary to provide work for the people.
Men and women must be given work. They are willing to work but they cannot get it. I can remember when I was a lad there were two or three jobs for every boy who wanted one. To-day we have a great multitude of the finest young men and women in the world, young Canadians, who are anxious to work. They are healthy, and the majority of them are very well educated. It is necessary to have a matriculation certificate to get any kind of job to-day.

Even a pick and
shovel job.

Even a pick and shovel
job, as someone suggests;. I am sure these young people and their parents will support any measure which the minister or the government of which he is a member may suggest in order to provide employment. I appeal to the minister to go the whole way. Let us get on with something in this country. We have been fooling with this matter altogether too loDg. It will be said: Where is the money going to come from? I have said that sometimes, but if war broke out to-morrow and Canada had to take a part, this government would soon get all the money required.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
And the next generation
would pay for it.

It will have to pay for
it anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member
was impressed with the amount stated the other day as being necessary for interest on outstanding debt. As I recall it, $136,000,000 was necessary to pay the interest on loans, most of which were incurred during the war years.

I was not here when
the budget speech was delivered, but I have since read it. In spite of what was said, my statement is not altered. If this country became involved in a war, which I hope it will not-I always contend that those who want war should be put in the front lines where they would be the first to suffer-the government would find the money. We are in a war, a colossal war against unemployment. Many people are suffering the pangs of war; they are suffering starvation and from depressed minds through inability to get work. This is particularly so of the young

Supply-Labour-Eeliej Works
folks. If war broke out to-morrow, the government would call them at once, so why not call them to work?
There is a great deal of necessary work to be done in this country. When the estimates of the minister in charge of lake levels and so forth were up the other day I stated that a tremendous amount of work was needed to be done in this country in that regard. Only yesterday I made a brief trip and I noticed that many of the rivers east of Toronto had overflowed their banks during the spring freshets. In the town of Port Hope alone over $100,000 worth of damage was done by the small river that flows through that municipality. Something ought to be done about it. The Ontario government does not seem to be big enough to grapple with it and it is up to this government in the last analysis to take steps to cope with this problem. The minister has a chance to live up to the reputation which the newspapers have given him and the nice things that have been said about him by members on all sides of the house. We all want to encourage him, for this is a time when any man who tries to do something should be encouraged.. Anything I say is not by way of criticism because I want to help the minister if I can. I say this to him however: Grapple with the subject in a big way. It is not for me to tell him how to do it; he can devise ways and means himself, and the government is strong enough and I believe big enough to grapple with it. I say, get after this problem in a big way. The sum of $9,000,000 is a very small one if the government is going to deal with this tremendous problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That is one of the many
items in the estimates.

I know, but this is the
item that has to do with new works in conjunction with the provinces. There is little leadership in the provinces; they are so overwhelmed with financial troubles that they are afraid to tackle anything big. I say therefore that this government should get in touch with the provinces and with those bodies throughout the country who are willing and anxious to suggest ways of providing real employment so that our idle men may be put to work. My hon. friend from Winnipeg referred to public buildings. That is one way, but personally I should like to see some works undertaken that would provide greater employment, and I should like to see more of the money voted paid out directly in wages. If we can save the country for another year or two I believe it would get on top again; but we must do everything we possibly can in the present trying period which we are passing through. I am not one of those who think that the depression is over. The parade in Toronto the other day -perhaps the same thing occurred in Montreal and Winnipeg-indicates clearly that there are still thousands out of work. The minister has behind him the best country in the world and the strongest government numerically this country ever had. He has only to ascertain what is to be done to be effective, and the house, irrespective of party, will support any measure whatever that has for its object the employment of Canadians.

What will be
the function of the national employment commission in regard to this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
This question was put in
a somewhat different form when the bill creating that commission was before the house. If I remember rightly I said then that if the commission were in a position to assist us in indicating the direction in which money should be expended, we should be very glad indeed to have their advice, but that with regard to expenditures for this year we should have to make provision ourselves and profit by the experience not only of the late administration but also of those provincial governments that have had to deal with relief works during the depression period. I think it is quite obvious that with respect to these particular expenditures they will be devoted in the main to highways, as has been done in past years. That is to say, under this item the works will be carried out in conjunction with the provinces, and the national employment commission will not be particularly concerned.
I suggest that when the agreements are being entered into with the provinces consideration be given to spending a portion of the amount in the elimination of railway level crossings.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Under the Department of Railways there is a special vote in connection with level crossings.

I have listened for
several days to a discussion of unemployment and have not said much, but there have been going through my mind certain ideas which I wish to place before the committee. It seems to me that the whole question is, how can we get our people back to work? Have we asked ourselves the question why there are so many unemployed in the coun-
Supply-Labour-Relie/ Works

try? What is the cause of this unemployment? If we could analyse the whole situation and find the cause we might decide on a remedy. It appears from the statement of the Minister of Finance that our hope of recovery lies in increased export markets. Is the loss of export markets the cause of unemployment? If so, why did we lose those markets? There is a reason. I think the committee will agree with me that the reason is that other countries began producing more of the goods which they needed and therefore there is not now the demand there used to be for imports from Canada. Not long ago I was reading a report from England which impressed me with the progress which the Minister of Agriculture there has made in the production of foodstuffs in England. There has been a vast increase. I was startled however to learn that during 1934, which showed very considerable progress as compared with 1933, there were 288,011 fewer people employed in agriculture in England than in the previous year. That report indicates that England at the present time can provide food for her own use for a considerable time-I forget how many days, but almost two hundred in the year. Compare that with production in 1913, when she could provide food for about thirty days only. That gives some idea of the progress that has been made there, and that with fewer people employed. I suggest that we should analyze the unemployment situation from that angle.
We have heard a good deal this session about the trade agreement with the United States and the great benefits that we shall derive from it. There may be more exports, but when there are more exports there must be more imports. We have found that already in the last returns. In the Easter recess I was out west where I talked to farmers who had fed cattle during the winter. They had stall-fed cattle and they told me that if instead of shipping them they had taken them out and shot them last fall they would be further ahead, for they did not receive the price of the feed. And since coming back I have heard the same story from several members. So that if a larger export market is to be the solution, things do not look very hopeful from that point of view.
I believe that the chief cause of unemployment in Canada is the advent of machinery, which has taken the place of workers. It is being done day by day in increasing measures all over the world, and if prosperity returns you will find machines coming in faster than ever they did in the past, with more employment as the result. The best brains in the

world to-day are trying to create unemployment by the improving of existing machines and the creating of new ones, and here we are, trying to solve the problem. It follows that there would be no unemployment if there were no machines. You must recognize that if the machine is here to stay we have to grapple with its products, and the first product of the machine is unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Has my hon. friend ever looked into the history of the poor law in Great Britain before the industrial revolution?
And the days of Caesar, when they had no machinery?

I am thinking of our own times. The hon. member who sat down a few moments ago referred to the time of his youth, and those of us who are threescore years old are in a position to compare the condition of youth then with its lot to-day. Forty years ago anyone who was honest and industrious could look forward to a measure of success. The youth of to-day has no such outlook.
How many members noticed in the press an account of the discharge by the Bank of England of one thousand of its clerks? The fact was reported in the Winnipeg paper two days before his late majesty King George gave his jubilee address. The bank laid off at one time a thousand clerks between the ages of twenty-six and thirty-four. The management had installed machines to take the place of those employees, and they said to them: We are laying you off, but we will give to each of you either ten thousand dollars or ten dollars a week as long as you live. Seven hundred of them took the ten thousand dollars; three hundred took the ten dollars a week for life. According to British insurance rates the life expectancy of those three hundred would be thirty-seven years, so at the rate of ten dollars a week the Bank of England will have to pay to them $5,500,000, and we know they will have to pay to the seven hundred $7,000,000. So they will pay in all $12,500,000 as retirement alowances because they have put in something to take the place of those men. It is a very generous offer, and indicates, I think, something that will have to be recognized by every country in the world, that if a machine takes the place of a worker, the machine must contribute in some way to his livelihood. That is something for the government to find ways and means of doing. The article went on to say that in the thirty-seven years that the

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
bank would pay out $12,500,000 it would make a gross saving in clerical wages of $55,000,000, the amount being based on what they would [DOT]otherwise have to pay to their staff.
The purpose of putting in a machine anywhere must be to save money. If money is saved by laying off workers, surely the replacing agency has a responsibility to the state. If someone robs a man coming from his work he is put in prison, but if a man puts in a machine and prevents someone from getting wages, he is banqueted and called a success. Therefore I say that the first product of the machine is unemployment. Whether or not the government can solve it by putting a -production levy or something of the kind *on the product of machinery to take care of men deprived of work, there is some ground, surely, for investigation, because the government has to take the first product of the machine-unemployment-and care for it, while the man who has caused that unemployment through-* the use of the machine is allowed to make what he can. The effect is very serious. We have heard a lot about it already during the session. The first object of a discharge worker is to try to find another job. His chances are remote, and even though he is successful in securing another position it is almost always at a reduced wage. The effects of this wage cutting are also very serious.
Consider, too, the youth problem, which has already been referred to. The effect upon the health of the people has been tremendous. I have just put in six years as superintendent of a hospital, and I tell you that if you want to find some of the results of unemployment you will find them in our hospitals, including those which deal with mental patients. And what effect is unemployment having on crime? I think it will be admitted that the consequences in this direction are very grave. If we find the cause of unemployment we should be able to arrive at some form of cure. The member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), in a speech the other evening, urged that production and consumption should be brought into equation the one with the other. There is the only solution that I know of-the monetizing of the productive wealth of this country and its distribution to the people according to their need. I do not want to go any further into that at the present time, except to say that the government should find a way to do it. A solution is possible; there is no doubt about that. Our late King George said "Surely the people of this country can solve problems like this." It is no use
drifting; it is no use going on with palliatives, which are only temporary; some solution must be found, but whether by way of the machine, as I have suggested, or otherwise, the government should get right after it.

Consideration of this item brings to mind the total of the items specified for the Department of Labour, and also brings into view the aggregate amount provided for in these special supplementary estimates. In round figures the total amount assigned to the labour department is $19,500,000. Of that amount, nine million dollars odd, the item under consideration, which is a very substantial part of the whole, is to be expended in cooperation with the provinces. That brings me to the total of the estimates as shown on page 18, and we find that it is made up of three columns, "projects already undertaken," "other projects," and "total." The grand total of all these is $131,161,143.42. I wish to point out to the committee that included in that grand total are two items, one, an amount of about $29,000,000 which it has been, pointed out has already been voted by this committee, so that as far as making provision for this year is concerned it may be disregarded. It is not new money, provided this year. Another item is the deficit of the Canadian National Railways, $39,000,000. Those two added together make about $69,000,000. That deficit of the Canadian National Railways has never before been considered as part of any scheme for the relief of unemployment. Therefore that $59,000,000 is to be taken off this total of $131,000,000. Then there is a further amount of $26,000,000, grants in aid of the provinces which may be for the relief of unemployment, but which in the past has been treated as a contribution for direct relief. With these sums subtracted the balance remaining is very small. The minister has said that he desires to be on firm ground, and that the amount provided in this item is based roughly upon an average of the expenditure of the last five years.
The minister wrote a biography of the Prime Minister, which I have read with a great deal of interest; it is an excellent work. In that book he pictures the right hon. gentleman as an expert in labour legislation and social questions, matters of this kind. His entry into the public sendee was as Deputy Minister of Labour, and the Minister of Labour tells during the many years which have intervened that the Prime Minister has given special study to these questions. The Minister of Labour himself has also given special study to social and economic questions. During these five years this problem has been with us, and has received critical study. Yet

the minister, desiring to be on firm ground, has nothing better to offer to this committee and this country than adopting for this item the average expenditure by his predecessors during the past five years, and if hon. members look back they will find that the expenditures follow along the same lines, farm placements and matters of much the same sort.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend any
other suggestions to offer?

I am not offering any
suggestions, but I say that what was done in the past must have been fairly sound; we must have been proceeding along pretty sane lines-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Some were; some were not.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I do not wish to deal at all with the general observations of my hon. friend. I may be permitted, however, to say this, without any complaint of unfairness, that this government in its general approach to the unemployment problem does not believe it can be dealt with immediately by any

single solution that might be devised. We did not come into office with any undertaking that we would end unemployment by such and such a date, or within any fixed period. We made it perfectly clear that we were going to try to deal with the problem upon the basis of reaching long range solutions by careful study of the entire situation. As a result of such examination of the situation as I have been able to give during the past few months I am convinced that long range study is absolutely essential. But is it not reasonable that in the meantime w7e should take such measures as we can to consolidate the existing situation-, having due regard to all that may be required to meet emergent . conditions, which we trust will not occur, during the coming year? We are doing that. AVith reference to these particular expenditures, we are proceeding, not in a way which the late administration discovered for itself, but along paths which -have been approved by the experience of, I might say, all countries confronted with the unemployment situation during the past five years. The late administration did not originate such policies as land settlement and resettlement, expenditures on highways, contributions to farm placement. There is little value in a controversy between this government and the late administration as to the credit for discovering this or that method for dealing with the unemployment situation, and I have tried to avoid a discussion on that basis. If my hon. friend wishes to discuss this whole problem on another plane I suppose I must meet him there, but I am not anxious to do so.
I would think not.

I do not understand so.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: But under previous legislation, as the hon. member knows, the government might have reached an agreement with a province on July 10, as a result of pressure might have entered into another on September 20 and, as a result of further pressure, into another on October 22. That would not be possible under this legislation.

Why not? Will the
minister explain where in the statute or in any other provision there is anything to prevent him from making one, two or three agreements with a province? I think he ought to be able to do this, if conditions develop which render it desirable in order to accomplish the object he has in view.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I think the limitation lies clearly in the appropriation. The appropriation is to be allocated to the different provinces. When we have entered into an agreement with a certain province, such agreement will exhaust the amount of the appropriation available for that province. But under previous legislation the amount available for any province was never exhausted, because there was no limit whatsoever upon what might be paid under the terms of the relief legislation.

I have taken little part in the discussion because I am not disposed to be critical simply for the sake of being critical. I have endeavoured to follow the statements of the minister to piece together the complete plan of the government with regard to unemployment relief, and to translate that plan into terms of immediate and actual benefit . for those now suffering the miseries of unemployment. I have in mind a statement made by the minister on a previous occasion to the effect that past methods have failed, and that unemployment in Canada has now developed persistent characteristics. I am at a loss to discover, and I should like some assurance from him in what respect the plan he has outlined represents definite progress.
I am exceedingly anxious that the expenditure of large sums such as that now before the committee should represent more clearly than before an investment in employment
rather than one in unemployment. For a moment I should like to consider not only the economic losses represented by unemployment, but the social losses, a phase of the situation which has not been given sufficient emphasis in our debates. The social loss is represented in the deterioration of the skill of our labour, the lowering of health standards and the general demoralization of our youth. Such losses demand immediate action and a definite mobilization of national resources.
I believe we should have some assurance from the minister that in the general policy now fully before the committee at least a substantial number of those now on relief in Canada will, before next winter, have an opportunity to secure that which they desire more than anything else, namely employment under proper working conditions and at a living wage. We should not be so reluctant to learn from the experience of other countries, and when I make that statement I have Sweden in mind. That nation has demonstrated its ability to maintain its living standards throughout the entire period of the depression. It has reduced unemployment to a point at which those unemployed represent less than one per cent of the population, and it has effected a revival of trade. I understand that part of its success is due to careful planning and coordination, and the central direction of expenditures such as those now under discussion. In the past the chief criticism of our policy has been lack of planning and lack of central direction and control.
The minister has suggested that there has been a lack of constructive criticism, and with that in mind may I remind him that on previous occasions we have suggested that the government should assume a more definite measure of responsibility in connection with the direction of expenditures of this type, having in mind the objective of a national plan. I have not yet discovered how these expenditures will be dealt with under the plan which, we hope, will be developed by the national employment commission. When I return to my constituency I shall have to meet the unemployed. Groups of them are organized at different points, and they will be anxious to know exactly what benefits will accrue to them and what opportunities they will be given to return to employment. I suggest that the minister should not complain if we ask of him a more definite assurance that in connection with the expenditures contemplated steps will be taken to work out a national plan to deal with a subject of

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My hon. friend will agree,
I think, that I had given an undertaking to answer his question in connection with another item, and if I went beyond the subject matter of item 336 it was simply because I was seeking to give him the information he desired. If the information I have given is not adequate and there is any further information I can give him, either in my office or here, I shall be only too glad to let him have it in so far as it is available.

I am perfectly satisfied. What I am particularly interested in comes under any one of these votes; it comes under this very vote which is now being discussed, an amount required to provide for unforeseen contingencies. I think that description could be correctly applied to all the items that have passed, for they are all unforeseen or perhaps to be correct unseen, inasmuch as there are no agreements and no understandings on conversations between federal and local governments. What I want to find out is this: Under this vote, which will apply to my own province and perhaps to my own constituency, if the provincial government should fail to contribute fifty per cent of the cost, can the Minister of Labour

Supply-Labour-Relief Works
assure the committee that, so far as the federal vote is concerned, the money voted will be expended where it was intended to be expended, and will be expended absolutely under the control of the minister who is in charge of the department concerned with that particular vote? If that happens, owing to the fact that the province either will not join or has not the money, the people who are in need will stand, when parliament prorogues, precisely where they are to-day. Perhaps the minister is not in a position to answer the question until he has had an opportunity of discussing it with the government. I am content to wait, but it is only in the interests of people who, I know, are suffering and are ready to work but cannot get work, that I am now asking the minister this question. I do not for a moment wish to hold up the estimate, but I should like to get an answer in order to find out the policy of the government in reference to moneys which we vote, which this parliament votes. If the provinces for any reason fail to give fifty per cent, is it the government's intention to have the money expended notwithstanding that contingency, provided the relief act will permit of this being done? If that act does not allow this, then it seems to me there will be a stalemate and the act will have to be amended at the present session. I do not press the minister for an immediate reply, but I submit that there should be a reply within a reasonable time after he has had an opportunity of discussing the matter with the Prime Minister and his colleagues with respect to general policy.
Will any restrictions be placed upon the provinces with regard to the kind of projects which they can undertake?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
We do not place any restrictions in advance upon the kind of projects that may be submitted. We rather deal with a program submitted by the province, the expenditure on which program in most cases would exceed the amount that would be available as a contribution of the dominion government. In other words, that would give the dominion government some opportunity to express a preference for one project rather than for another, because

obviously we must see to it that the projects which are adopted will be those that will contribute as far as possible to employment.
Do I understand that in the final analysis it will be the federal government that will determine the projects to be proceeded with?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: To this extent, that the federal government obviously determines the projects to which it will contribute, and in the nature of things if the provinces wish to secure the federal contribution they will try to reach an agreement. In fact, that will be the desire on both sides.

Suppose that in some of the provinces it is thought that as a relief project nothing will produce better results than, say a housing scheme; would such a scheme meet with the approval of the Department of Labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am unable to give an assurance on that point in advance of its being submitted to the federal government by a province, but I do not think there has been any anticipatory restriction upon the programs that might be submitted by the provincial government. It is for the dominion government to seek to work out, in cooperation with the provincial governments, a program of projects best adapted to improve the relief situation in the particular province.
Are the municipalities being asked to share any part of the burden?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is
aware, the dominion government has not dealt direct with the municipalities. It may be that in some provinces certain projects will be put forward which will involve the construction of municipal works, but when it has been proposed that the dominion government should contribute to municipal works the proposal has always come through the province, and the dominion contribution has always been upon a lower percentage basis.

May I ask if the amount
being contributed by the federal government in regard to these undertakings will be by way of a loan or a gift from the federal authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Under this particular item

Yes.

The total monthly grant
in aid prior to December, 1935, was $1,751250. Under the increases authorized for the winter months, December to March inclusive, the total monthly grant in aid was $3,066,218.75. What is $26,000,000 divided by twelve? I make it $2,166,666. How is the minister going to pay $2,606,285 per month out of $26,000,000 voted?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am not sure that it is possible to give a definite answer to the question which is at least implied in what my right hon. friend has said. We are making here an estimate of what will be required for direct relief as a contribution from the dominion government during the coming year. There has been, as he is aware, a reduction of fifteen per cent announced for the month of April. We assume that some other adjustment may be desirable as the relief situation is studied during the ensuing months. We are resolved at all events to meet the situation as it develops. This sum of $26,000,000 is an estimate of what we hope and trust will not be exceeded as a contribution from the dominion government during the present fiscal year. That is undoubtedly so. But the minister must have a lot of faith if he thinks he is going to pay $2,606,285 a month for a year out of $26,000,000. speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I can only remind the committee that the monthly contributions by the dominion to the provinces have not been fixed for the entire fiscal year. The reduction announced for April 1 was one which applied to that month and has been continued to date, but there was no assurance or undertaking that there would not be further adjustments of the dominion grant in aid to the provinces. I believe that in the past it was on a month to month basis; that is to say, there was no agreement that the grant in aid would be continued through the year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, we did make an agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
With some provinces, I believe, that was the case.

speechtext: I doubt whether I can give such an assurance, and if I could I doubt whether it would be wise to do so. We have attempted to make an estimate of the amount which we believe will be required during the coming year as a dominion contribution to the provinces for direct relief. I should like to repeat this further statement, which I made before six o'clock, that we are at the same time resolved to meet the situation as we believe the people of Canada would wish us to meet it, as it may alter from time to time.
Under the unemployment relief act as it now stands, can a grant in aid be made without having to come to parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The relief bill of the present fiscal year, section 4, states:
The governor in council may enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein and providing for any payments on account of such relief measures to be made out of moneys appropriated for relief purposes by parliament for the fiscal year 1936-37.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Under the special supplementary estimates our grants for relief purposes are limited to the 126,000,000 therein stated.
I think the hon. gentleman is trying to find out how it would be possible for the government under the bill to give a larger amount than $26,000,000 for grants in aid.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: If that is the question, 1 can only say that parliament will be in session again before the close of the present fiscal year. I had that in view when I said that in any event the government is resolved to meet the situation as it develops.

I am not objecting to this amount. As a matter of fact I think the government would be unwise to tie its hands so that in a very uncertain situation it could not deal with any conditions which might arise. Regardless of what the policy of the government may be I do not think it is so tied.
How does this amount compare with the amount of grants in aid during the past fiscal year?

speechtext: As they stood prior to December, 1936, the total annual contribution by the dominion government for direct relief was $21,000,000 in round figures. speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext:
The minister
might explain this item at some length so that we may understand what is proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It was decided as a matter of government policy that an attempt should be made to provide work for those single unemployed men who have been, some of them for some years, in the relief camps, and it was considered that at least one item of useful work would be to assist the railways in picking up their deferred maintenance work, such work to be in addition to the usual maintenance program of the railways. The government consulted the railways, and the respective railway managements stated that they could usefully employ about 5,000 men during the present season.
That is 5,000 apiece?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, 10,000 in all. A good deal of discussion took place as to how this would work out from the standpoint of both the rail-ways and the government, and it was found that each would have to spend about an equal amount of money. That is, if the government paid the wages of these 10,000 men, the railways would be called upon to spend another $3,100,000 for supervision, supplies, materials, and other details having to do with work. So agreements have been entered into between the government and the Canadian Pacific and between the government and the Canadian National Railways providing that the government will furnish up to 5,000 men for each railway. It is understood of course that the 5,000 may not be available for each railway because the men might prefer other employment. The men will be employed by the railway at the standard rates of wages for the class of work they are called upon to do. The government will pay in full the wages of the men while thus employed by the railway on this particular class of work.

Where track has been laid, for instance, but no ballasting done, will the men be available for that class of work or only for the maintenance of old work already completed?

speechtext: I do not know that there is any specific prohibition against using the men on new track, but this is chiefly for maintenance of way work on road already constructed and in use, such as ditching, track laying, and work of that sort.

Are we now to understand that all these men who have been laid off by the railways themselves are to be reemployed and that in addition each railway requires
5,000	men?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext:
I have now the explanation. Assuming that the government can furnish
10,000	men the money is all spent for labour, but naturally the government cannot guarantee to furnish 10,000 men from this source, and provision is therefore made that if we furnish a lesser number, say 5,000, the railways shall be reimbursed for the expenditures they have made in preparing work for 10.000. bour. speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
As this item is closely related to a policy announced by the Department of Labour, perhaps I might be permitted to say a few words in answer to my hon. friend. When it was announced that the government proposed to close the relief camps conducted by the Department of National Defence, it was stated1 to be a definite part of that proposal that these men would not be turned out of these camps without some pro-

vision being made for their future. I think that was fully understood by the house and I am quite sure my hon. friend would be the first to accept such a view.
Absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: There were two methods by which we could proceed. We could continue necessary work on existing projects until July 1 and pay the men an increased allowance during that period. At the time we made our plans there were some 20,000 men in the relief camps and we realized that it would be essential to make some large provision for additional employment after July 1, the date set for the closing of the camps. After careful investigation we concluded that work on maintenance of way upon the railways was a direction in which employment could be afforded to provide assistance to the men as well as greatly to improve the railroads which improvement in turn would add to the travelling comfort of our people. We have every reason to believe that the relief camps will be able to supply these 10,000 men. My hon. friend brings up the question of other men without employment not having the same opportunity for this employment-
Not exactly. What I said was: Assuming that there were not 10,000 men available from the relief camps, would persons not in the camps be debarred from making up that total of 10,000?

speechtext: As I recall it, the understanding is .that the railway companies will take up to 10,000 men from the relief camps. I state that, subject to correction as to the precise terms of the agreements to be made with the railway companies. What I wanted to bring out was that this is simply part of a general plan to bring the relief camps to a close.
Have the agreements not been made?
