speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

Do I gather from the
Minister of Labour that the railways are interested in .the source from which these men come and wish them to come from the relief camps? I think the men to be chosen should come under the much wider category in subsection 2 of section 3 of Bill No. 19 which reads:
-for the employment of persons who being available and competent are necessarily and properly in receipt of relief in the province in which such work or undertaking is to be performed.
There now seems to be some limit in connection with the 5,000 men to be supplied to each railway. Is it the understanding that they are to come from the relief camps lately under the direction of the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, that is definitely the
understanding. Of course we are contributing this labour to the railways. That is, we are paying the cost of it because we feel that this is a measure to supplant these relief camps.
Is the government paying the whole cost of the wages to these men?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, all the wages to the
men.

How much will be spent
by both railways and the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext:
Everyone who knows
anything about maintenance of way work on the railways knows that labour constitutes at least four-fifths of the cost of this work. I assume that if the railway companies are going to spend dollar for dollar with the government, they will employ considerably more than the 10,000 men to come from the relief camps, or they will be charging against their account exorbitant rates for haulage, shovels and the like in connection with the gravel pits. As I say, over four-fifths of the cost of work done on maintenance of way on the established lines is for labour, so in order to spend dollar for dollar the railway companies will have to employ at least double the number of the men that are to be provided by the government. If they propose to keep on the same number of men this
year as they have had in other years on maintenance work, this will necessitate their having at least 20,000 men. That would take up the 10,000 men from the camps, plus another 10,000 men. I should like to know if the government, through its employment agencies, is to have any say in connection with the extra men to be employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My hon. friend says "everyone knows," but I shall have to make some exceptions to that. The Minister of Railways does not know; his deputy does not know and his chief engineer does not know. We checked very carefully the figures that we put before us and we found that if the supervision

The supervision will be
high.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There will be the men required to supervise the work; there will be the materials required for the work as there is a considerable amount of ballasting to be done, and there will be the cost of equipment. The figures I have given appear to present the true picture.

Is any provision being made with regard to unemployed railway men in the various towns? If the railways are being subsidized to this extent-and I was not aware that the government was to bear the whole cost of the wages-I should think something ought to be done to try to get the railways to take on unemployed railway men. There are hundreds of them in the cities and in some of the smaller centres. Even in the little town of Biggar in my constituency there is a number of railway men who have been almost altogther out of work for several years. Cannot something be done in their behalf when the railways are being subsidized? If we are to embark upon the subsidizing of institutions for the purpose of employing men, the railways are not the only ones that should be considered. We have a bill for the rehabilitation of agriculture and I believe a great deal of unemployed labour could be used advantageously in assisting to clear land which has already been settled in order that the settlers may become self-supporting. That would be a valuable form of the utilization of such subsidized labour. However the specific question I am asking at the moment is: What is to become of unemployed railway men in these towns? Is anything going to be done to give these men employment in view of the subsidy given the railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is a distinct understanding with both the railways that the ordinary maintenance crews will be employed before

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
this type of labour is utilized by the railways. I think my hon. friend will agree that the railway man who has seniority should be given the first opportunity of seeking employment on extra crews. I doubt very much whether the hundreds of men he speaks of will not be offered work on extra gangs during the summer months. That includes any man with seniority.
Will a copy of the agreement be/tween the two railways and the government be tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The agreement has not yet been executed. It has been signed by the railway companies but the government has not signed it because it has not the authorization.
Is each railway to get the same number of men?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, that is the provision.

In many of the towns there is a great number of young single men, now out of employment who were employed by the railways some years ago. They were laid off and they have been waiting year after year for brighter times in the hope of being reemployed on the railways. I understand that in Nova Scotia at a certain point, the terminal at Point Tupper, there are many unemployed men who worked on the railways in years gone by, and under this scheme it is the intention to send men from God knows where, from the relief camps, to work at this point, while these men who have been" waiting for years with their mouths open will get no employment at all. I do not desire to criticize any scheme which the government is strenuously putting forward to alleviate the unemployment situation, but I really do not think it is fair that men who are now out of employment should be handicapped because they refused to become a public charge, to go into the camps or to take relief. It seems to me to -be rather unfair that because of this refusal, because of their independence and possibly because of a little pride-and I wish there were a little more pride left in many people-these men are now to be penalized. They did not choose to go into detention camps, though if they had gone there they would now be eligible for employment, whereas under this scheme it would appear that they are to be penalized for not having become a public charge.

On the Canadian National at Fort William there are men working who have not worked so early in the season in

years. I know these men personally and I can say that usually they do not get work until well on in the summer. Now they are engaged in regular work with wages.

I do not know whether it is wise to ask more questions on this item; the more questions I ask the more confused I am. Whether it is because I am dense or because the answers are not clear I do not know. Do I understand the minister to say that the whole of the item of $3,100,000 is to be paid in wages to the men who are to do the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is correct.
What is meant by paragraph (d) which has been read by the acting leader of the opposition? Where is the appropriation for that item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Under certain conditions, to pay for materials?

Yes. I am referring to paragraph (d), which mentions materials and certain other expenditures. If the whole of this money is to go in wages there will be nothing left for materials and there is nothing further on in the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
What I attempted to say
was that that wras a saving clause for the government. In the event of our falling lamentably short of the supply of 10,000 men whom we have asked the railways to be prepared to use, we have provided for recouping the railways for such loss as they may incur in consequence of our failure to supply the number of men.

Why should there be any loss even if the government could not find a sufficient number of men in the unemployment relief camps? Could not either the government or the railways advertise for men to do the work? Is there any reason in the present state of the labour market why they should not find the men? I assume that this work is necessary; that the railway companies must perform it if they are to keep their tracks in proper repair; if they are going to this expense it must be because the work must be done. Either that is the situation, or the government is making them a free gift of a certain amount of work, not necessary, in order to keep men employed. That seems to be the only construction to which this item is open as it stands. There is no reason in the world why the government should have to pay for materials. As

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
this item stands, the government furnishes the money to pay the men; the men do the work, and the railways are going to receive all the relief given.

I think the reason I
am under the misapprehension that the railways as well as the government were contributing to the wages to be paid is my misunderstanding of the statement of the Minister of Labour on February 26, in which he said in part:
This work will be in addition to the usual maintenance work of the railways. It will be undertaken on a cooperative basis, provision for which will be proposed in the emergency supplementary estimates. Men taken from the relief camps by the railroads will be in private employment and on a basis of work and wages.
I certainly took that to mean that under the cooperative effort the railway companies and the government were going to contribute to the wages. That apparently is not what the minister meant.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I think it is a cooperative
basis. My hon. friend, as an engineer, will know that to do work of any kind requires both men and material. In this case the railways furnish the material, the supervision and the equipment of all kinds and stand the costs in connection therewith. The government pays the costs of direct labour of the men it furnishes to the railways. Therefore I think the statement of the Minister of Labour was accurate.

I should like
the Minister of Railways to enlighten us on this point. I know that the agreement cannot legally be put through until authority is given by parliament. But the draft is ready and has been signed by the railways. Does it provide that only men from the relief camps can be used for this purpose, or, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North suggested, if there are not enough men from the relief camps, who are to work there? Is there any provision by which other unemployed men can be used for this purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The railways agree to
utilize men furnished them by the government. We propose to take those men from the relief camps.
Only?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
But if we wish to extend
that further, there is nothing in the agreement to prevent our doing so.

Still, the government
will pay the wages.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Quite; if we furnish the men to the railways we pay their wages.

What is the
purpose of the government with regard to this particular point? Do they intend to pay the wages only of men who have come from the relief camps, or, if there are not sufficient of those, do they intend to pay the wages of other unemployed?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I think it has been made sufficiently clear that under the work as contemplated we propose to supply these men from the relief camps up to a maximum of
10,000	men. If there should not be 10,000 men available from the relief camps, it is within the terms of the agreement as I understand it that they can be supplied from other sources, and I need not remind the right hon. gentleman that there are relief hostels in our larger cities from which the additional number could be supplied without any difficulty whatsoever. As a matter of fact, upon the basis of progress made thus far, we do not anticipate that there will be difficulty in supplying the 10,000 men from the relief camps. That was the original object of the plan. It is bound up in an integral way with our whole plan of closing the relief camps as from July 1.

Looking at this amount and all the items, including compensation, transportation, overhead, material and so on, the cost of the 10,000 men will run to about $300 a head. The question I am asking is this: Are these men paid wages and then will they pay the company board? Or will the company board them and the government simply pay an amount of wages? In other words, is the company making a contribution by way of board and lodging and the government paying the wages, or will the government also pay the board of these men? Or will the board be deducted from the men's wages? If so, has a basis of such deduction been arrived at between the government and the railway companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The men will be furnished in exactly the same way as any other people who are employed by the railway on the same class of work. There will be no special privileges or exemptions or anything else; they are just men returning to the ordinary occupations of life, employed in the ordinaiy way, paid wages in the ordinary way, exactly as any other men who are employed on extra gang work for railways.

Supply-Railways-Relief Works

Could the
minister inform us whether under this item the railway companies could undertake such work as reconditioning freight and passenger cars, locomotives and equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The work is restricted entirely to maintenance of way work, extra gang work. In railway circles extra gang work is very clearly defined as work on tracks.
Is it the policy of the government to utilize all the men in the unemployment camps before any unemployed railway men will be taken care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We seem to be working in circles. I explained some time ago that all normal railway employment will be utilized before we recruit any men from the relief camps. That is just the opposite of what my hon. friend suggests.

May I ask the minister if
under the terms of this agreement the railways will have the authority to dismiss men who are not found satisfactory? In addition to that, will they be replaced by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Of course the railways must be permitted to dismiss men who are not satisfactory. Whether they are replaced or not will, I suppose, be optional with the government. In other words, if they are not replaced we shall not be held responsible for the wages.

What is the connection between this particular vote and item 427, which provides for a loan of about $1,100,000 to the railways, presumably for this same work? Is that $1,100,000 a part of the $3,100,000 which we are putting up under item 419, or what is the explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is in order to explain a vote that we have yet to come to, but I should be very glad to do so. The difficulty of making this agreement with the railroads was that when we first approached them they both had had their budgets for 1936 approved, and no provision had been made for the railroads' portion of this item, amounting to about $3,000,000 for the two railways. In order to facilitate the making of the agreements, we undertook to finance the railways for a short period for the portion of the railroads' part of the expenditure that will be for labour, that is the labour of supervision and the skilled labour

used in operating the equipment necessary to put these men at work. It is purely in the nature of a loan with interest to the railways for a short period to permit them to take advantage of this situation.

Another matter is not clear to my mind. I understood the Minister of Labour to say a moment ago that all the men in the relief camps would first be absorbed. Now I understand the Minister of Railways to say that the unemployed railway men will be taken care of first. I represent a large railway town, Smith's Falls, in which there is a large number of unemployed railway men. It would seem only right and proper that if work is to be done on the railways these unemployed railway men should be taken care of before outsiders are taken on. If I am not mistaken, the Minister of Labour said a moment ago that the unemployed men in the camps would be taken care of first.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Out of the 10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Perhaps I can make this clear. This vote has nothing whatever to do with the ordinary maintenance work on the railways. In other words the railways continue with ordinary maintenance work with their usual forces, and I think my hon. friend will agree that, as I explained before, any man with seniority on the railway has been employed during the last summer or two on maintenance of way or extra gang work. This procedure will be followed first; and it is entirely aside from this problem. This work is entirely apart and in addition to any ordinary maintenance of way work of the railways. The first men to be employed for this additional gang work, which is to be separately organized in every way, will be the men from the relief camps, as my colleague the Minister of Labour has said.

Is it going to be the policy of the government to take men from the relief camps, place them in employment with private companies and pay their wages with government funds? If so, and if there is any surplus of men left in the relief camps, have the government any idea what they are going to do with those men? Would they consider putting them at work like farming and in that way subsidizing the farmers of western Canada? This looks like a gift to the railways as far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I believe that same question arose during the discussion on the estimates of the Department of Labour. In addition to providing this extra gang work for 10,000 of

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
those formerly in relief camps, we are also making every effort to secure employment for the remaining men in the relief camps, and from the decrease in the strength in the relief camps during the past few months we have reason to believe that these efforts have been quite successful. Apart from that, my hon. friend will perhaps recall that the wage allowance for those who will be engaged in relief camp projects until July 1 has been increased, so that when the men leave the relief camps on July 1, they will at least have some stake for industrial reestablishment.
But what I want to know is whether the government's efforts will include the subsidizing of these men in employment, or is it intended just to let them shift for themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am not sure that I understand the distinction. We are maintaining employment for these men in relief camps until July 1, so far as they do not find employment with the railway companies under the plan now before the committee.
But the minister said that efforts would be made to place these men in employment. Does the effort include subsidizing some classes of society to pay their wages?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The answer is no.

I do not think we should let this item pass without frankly admitting that we are subsidizing the two railways to the amount of $3,100,000.
Mr. FINN; Hear, hear.

Namely, $1,550,000 to the Canadian Pacific and $1,550,000 to the Canadian National. It is a straight cash subsidy to the two railways in the form of wages of labour on maintenance of way work. We may as well frankly face the situation; this committee and the country ought to note that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is benefiting to the extent of $1,550,000. It is about time also that the Canadian people realized that the Canadian National has been vilified up and down the country for the last six years, antil it is to me amazing that the officers of that railway have been able to carry on at all. Furthermore we are subsidizing them to the extent of another million dollars by another item. That makes $4,209,400 that the government is giving as a subsidy to the railways.
The hon. member asks what I think is a very proper question. The government is going to subsidize the Canadian Pacific for its
maintenance of way work, which is two years overdue. Ride from here to Winnipeg on that railway and you get thrown out of your seat, whereas that road used to be in excellent shape. The Canadian Pacific is two years behind its normal track work program. To talk about this being extra, above all that is necessary, is sheer nonsense. The Canadian Pacific is being given a subsidy of $2,000,000 for maintenance of way work of which it is in dire need. It is time that the people of Canada know we are playing the part of a pretty good friend to the Canadian Pacific, and there is no reason why we should not subsidize some other industries, or the farm-era of this country, to take care of 5,000 men from the camps.
And the fishermen.

And the fishermen, too. I deplore the suggestion that we are not giving a special favour to these railways, because we are. Of course to the Canadian National we hand out money pretty generously, in any case; we supply the capital, but we ought to make it abundantly clear that in this vote we are subsidizing the Canadian Pacific for ordinary maintenance of way work, long past due, to keep their trains from rocking off the tracks; that is what it amounts to. Furthermore, it will take a whole lot more than $2,000,000 to put their tracks into normal condition. I say that without fear of successful contradiction. I am not objecting to this vote at all; I would not object to doubling it; I commend the Minister of Labour for the scheme of getting the camps closed and the men into useful work. But I would enlarge that tremendously; I would subsidize the putting of men to work in this country, as my hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) said this afternoon. I would subsidize putting them to work on reforestation. Look at the pitiful little vote for grade separation, $1,000,000. Make it $5,000,000 and do a real job; save a few lives as well as increase employment. Before this session is ended I am going to have something to say about where the money would come from; I am not at all afraid of that. This talk about where the money is to come from, when human lives are going to the devil every day for want of a bit of employment, does not frighten me. It is about time, as the Minister of Finance said the other day, to look facts in the face. There are some other facts to look in the face; this fact that we are subsidizing the Canadian Pacific as well as the Canadian National ought to be noted and well noted in this country.

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
By the way, the Minister of Finance made the statement the other day that we have done everything the British authorities have done except balance the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no, no.
Well, I am not very far wrong. Read the words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know very well what I said.
All right, we will pause for a moment and.find it. I am not far out, and I am quite willing to be checked, because I think it will sound quite as well in the minister's language as in mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quite sure of that.
Will the minister tell me what he did say?
The hon. member had better read it.

If I have time to find it, I will read it. In any case the minister said that we had done virtually all the British had done, with the exception of balancing the budget. While he is looking his statement up-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me read what I did say.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I refer to page 2384 of Hansard. Although this is not the budget debate, I believe I should be given an opportunity to make this quotation. I suppose these and other words of mine will be duly and extensively criticized within the next few days.
I am not criticizing them. I am citing them as an authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The words are these:
I am well aware that this will be called a doctrine of deflation. Indeed, I have heard it said recently that Canada has been following a policy of "heroic deflation" and that she should take a leaf out of the book of the mother country. It is not easy for me to understand how departure from the gold standard, recurring deficits, financing by borrowing, of the magnitude of these which I have outlined, and a monetary policy which has allowed the Canadian dollar to fluctuate approximately at par with the managed Sterling standard and with the devalued United States dollar and which has made possible an expansion of the country's cash base just as rapidly as that of Great Britain, can be described as deflation. More careful analysis would rather appear to indicate that in those financial matters about the only point in the British program which we have not already adopted is her policy of keeping the budget balanced.
[Mr, Stevens.l
That is practically what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh!
No.
Practically what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of fact, it reads better than I thought it did.

It was written, so naturally it agrees. Let me tell the minister that I was citing it for this reason: We talk about doing what the British have done. The government is subsidizing the Canadian Pacific Railway to repair its right of way. That is what we are doing to-night. Why not do what the British have done and subsidize some of our industries to enable them to reemploy workmen in their industries? Assist them in going so far as to relocate; move them from one place to another. That is a part of the British program that we do not have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
appreciate that in this instance I specifically referred to the financial problem.
And that is her financial problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, I see.
That is part of the British financial problem of which we are not taking notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not a financial
problem at all.

Absolutely, it is. It comes out of their general provision for financing for unemployment; that is what it does. We are doing nothing in that respect, with the exception of this matter for which I commended the minister some weeks ago. In so far as it accomplishes the return of men to normal employment, it is good and it is commendable. But do not let us blind our eyes to the fact that it is a straight subsidy to the Canadian Pacific Railway as well as to our own Canadian National Railways, and I can see no reason in the world why the hon. member's question, asked a minute ago, is not a reasonable one. Why should we not extend the subsidizing of private corporations from the Canadian Pacific Railway to other industries, if you like? It may be to the lumber industry; it may be to the factories and it may be, as I said a minute ago, by way of an enlarged vote for grade separation. Why should we not subsidize some of these almost bankrupt municipalities in which there are extremely dangerous level crossings? Of what use will $1,000,000 be in the work of

Sup-ply-Railways-Relief Works
grade separation? Some of this work is costly, and we could spend 85,000,000 to the greatest advantage. I should like to say to the government that I believe it is their duty earnestly to face that situation and to recognize the reasonableness of this question: Why should we not subsidize some other lines of industry, in addition to the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In fairness to the railways permit me to say that this is not a subsidy to the railways in any way, shape or form. This government had a serious problem on its hands. There were from 10,000 to 20,000 men in the relief camps, the numbers fluctuating with the seasons. Those camps cost the country 89,000,000 in the past year. The men are performing work which, to say the least is hardly commensurate with the cost of maintenance of the camps. For a number of years conditions in those camps have been the subject of complaint, and there has been considerable discontent in them. Some of our authorities consider them a serious menace to peace and order.
Faced with that problem the government went to the railway companies and asked their assistence. In handling the problem it was necessary to have large scale employment within the capacity of men in the relief camps, and by that I mean work which would require perhaps less than the average ability of the men. It is necessary to have the men work under supervision, and work under an organization capable of handling 10,000 men, using decent equipment and working under good conditions. As I say, work was required which would put the men on a basis of equality with other workers in the same class of employment.
We went to the railways with that problem and asked for their help. I may say that they found it rather difficult to help, because their budgets for the year had been brought down, and the employment of large numbers of men required large expenditures, for which they had made no provision. The railways went as far as we could reasonably ask them to go, and in order that they might be enabled to bear their full share we had to help them out by way of loans. But after the railways had come to the aid of the government, as they have, I must object seriously to any man saying in the House of Commons that we are subsidizing the Canadian Pacific Railway, or our own road the Canadian National Railways.

The minister may object if he likes, but that does not end the matter by any means. It is all very well for him to 12739-159
say that the government had a problem. Of course they had a problem. No person criticizes them in that respect, and I am commending the minister and the government for having worked out the problem, so far as it has been worked out. But to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways are doing this country a favour by accepting 84,000,000 in restoration of their degenerated-I think that is the best word-
Reconstruction.

-right of way is, I think, sheer nonsense. The minister may take objection to what I say, and to the way I put it, but I know what I am talking about. Both railway companies are in dire need of restoration and maintenance of way work. They are in very serious need of it, and everybody knows it. By the way, one or two members spoke aibout the placing at work of the maintenance of way gangs of the railways. I want to say to the hon. member who appeared to know what he was talking about, and to the hon. member for Fort William, that neither of these railways is restoring its maintenance of way gangs to normal conditions. They may be doing just about one-tenth of the normal work, as they have been doing in the last four or five years. But when hon. members talk about normal maintenance of way work carried on by the railway companies may I say that if it were undertaken it would easily absorb 10,000 men, without a dollar from the government. The railways are not doing that. If the agreement calls for it, and the minister and government will check on it, they will find that a few thousand more men will have work than those for whom provision has already been made.
The minister has objected to my observations, and I take just as strenuous objection to any person who gives out the impression that the Canadian Pacific Railway have come to us, like philanthropists, and have taken
5,000	men off our hands. What that railway is doing is this: It is accepting 82,000,000 from the taxpayers of Canada to help it pay normal expenditures incurred in connection with its right of way. That is what it is doing, and it is not fair to the taxpayers of Canada to suggest anything else.
I had no intention of making these observations, but to-day and other days I have listened to the suggestion that we, the parliament of Canada, were receiving some great favour from the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways because we were being permitted to pay the cost of their



Supply-Railways-Relief Works
maintenance of way work. I think it is about time that the country should realize that in this and in other respects we have been very kind to the Canadian Pacific. I am not criticizing that at all; I am quite willing to be kind, but I am not willing to be kind to the Canadian Pacific much longer if they abuse the Canadian National Railways the way they have been doing during the last four or five years. It is about time that the taxpayers of this country who own the Canadian National Railways should realize that they have a good plant and a valuable asset. True it was overbuilt, overextended, but let us look also at the overextension of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Some of these days, when I have an opportunity, I shall indicate some of those facts. I think it is about time that we had a little consideration for the Canadian National railway system, and that the country should recognize that it does not owe to the Canadian Pacific Railway any very great debt of gratitude for accepting two million dollars or so in this case, four or five million dollars in another case, and a loan of sixty million dollars in another case. Let us recognize that we have been a fairy godmother to the Canadian Pacific Railway as well as to the Canadian National Railways.

I have
listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the last speaker, but I scarcely think they are germane to the matter before the committee. I am intensely interested in the question raised by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLennan). If I followed the Minister of Railways this vote is to take care of 10,000 men from the relief camps, and their employment is not to interfere with the ordinary maintenance work of the railways in each season. Along the line of railway with which I am familiar-and I suppose my experience is no.t different from that of other members-not only does that ordinary work include the usual maintenance work of the railway, but every spring a considerable number of extra men is taken on who, although not permanent, are dependent for employment on that class of labour. But during the last few years, owing to the economies put into effect, their employment has been more intermittent than usual. I am anxious to know whether this extra work will interfere with that class of labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Perhaps I should read from
the agreement which has been signed by the railway companies but not by the government:
The company will arrange to extend its program of maintenance of way and betterment work during the season of 1936 so as to

provide employment on its line of railway for approximately five thousand men in addition to those who would otherwise be engaged in such work during the said season, and will as far as practicable carry out such work over a period of from four to six months but so that the wages of such additional men will not exceed in the aggregate the sum of $1,502,450.
So the agreement states definitely that these men will be in addition to the men who would otherwise have been employed during the season.

What year do they base
that on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not know that they
base it on any year. It is 1936 requirements, I assume.

Is the maintenance work
this year going to be equal to that of last year or of those years when times were good?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is in addition to the men
they would ordinarily have employed in 1936.

There is a good deal of
difference between the number employed in 1929 and in 1935.

Mr. Chairman, may we
ask now that the minister table the agreement because it is one of the recognized rules that any document a minister quotes from shall be tabled? There can be no objection to tabling the agreement because it is signed by both companies and merely awaits, I suppose, the authority of the statute which is before the house. We would have a more intelligent idea of the matter if the agreement were tabled, and it would probably save a good deal of trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to
table the agreement as soon as it is completed.
Will the wage cheques be actually issued by the government or by the railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
By the railways, and they
will be reimbursed by the government.

Might I ask if the government has considered the plan of deferred wages such as they have now in the relief camps? I would suggest that this would be a good plan because after these men have worked a few months, if no part of their pay is held back, a great many of them will be back upon the country again; whereas under the deferred payment plan, if twenty-five per cent of their wages was withheld until the end of the season, and paid to them on

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
leaving when the work was all finished, they would have something to tide them over the winter months. If that is not done I am afraid that at the end of the season a great many of them will find themselves in exactly the same position as when they started work in midsummer, and the consequence will be that they will continue to be a charge upon the country and probably land back in the relief camps whence they came.
Does the agreement state what the rate of wages will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It will be the standard rate
of wages paid by the railways for the class of work the men are doing.

From the answer of the
minister to the question asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Riggar (Mr. Coldwell), I do not yet know who is going to pay the board of these men. Will the $300, roughly, which will reach each of these men be after board is deducted, or will they have to pay their board out of that $300? If the latter is the case, I do not think the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. McCann) need worry very much about deferred pay because the men will not have very much left.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
How does my hon. friend
arrive at his computation?
Ten thousand into

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This employment is from four to six months.
That makes it worse.

During the period each
will get about $300.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is the ordinary wages for
track men, which I believe is twentydive cents an hour in some sections and thirty-five cents an hour in others; that is for ordinary labour. Board, of course, is provided by the men. I may say in answer to my hon. friend opposite that the question of holding back part of the wages was considered, but we decided that as we were trying to get these men back to active private life, it would be improper to distinguish between the men ordinarily employed by the railways and the men taken from the camps. We wished to rid the minds of these men, some of whom have been looked after by the government for several years of the idea that they were wards of the government. Otherwise it might be hard 12739-159i
for them to understand that they were on their own resources. If they want to squander their money, as my hon. friend suggests, they will have to reap the rewards of that sort of thing.

I object to being termed, "hon. friend opposite." Our criticism is intended to be helpful. I agree with the minister when he says that we cannot make saints of men, whether they are in the labour camps or on the railways. They have as much right as we have to be foolish in spending their money. My concern is that the labour situation, especially in the municipalities along the lines of railways, shall' not be made more difficult by bringing in? these men from the relief camps. I know it is a difficult problem with which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Howe) have to deal, but my contention is that the problem should not be made more difficult for the municipalities through which the railways pass.

I did not catch the exact words of the agreement with the railways. The minister referred to certain specific purposes such as the betterment of roads and so on, but I should like to have the exact language.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The agreement reads:
The company will arrange to extend its program of maintenance of way and betterment work during the season of 1936 so as to provide employment on its line of railway for approximately 5,000 men in addition to those who would otherwise be engaged in such work during the said season.
How much goes to the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Half of the amount, or Sl,-
550,000.

I agree with many of th< statements made by the leader of the recon struction party (Mr. Stevens). It is quits true that that party is not very large, but while they did not succeed numerically, they sent the best brains in the party to the house. For that reason I compliment them. It seems to me that the leader of the reconstruction party is largely right and partly not wrong. He takes a view different from that which I take. I do not think this parliament or this country is under any obligation to the Canadian Pacific Railway to warrant our placing money directly in its hands. That railway is not poor; it never has been poor; it is rich in lands; it is rich in assets; in some directions it is rich in brains although to some extent the greatest brains are underneath the

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
ground. I am afraid that they are, shall I say, stooping to underground methods. What do we find when we read the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway? After applying $3,500,000 on the depreciation of their ocean steamships, which are under a separate corporation, the Canadian Pacific Ocean Steamships Limited, with a European manager who was recently knighited and who lives in London, they show profits of $1,348,526.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In my opinion the hon. member is out of order. The time will come when he can discuss the Canadian Pacific Railway, but I think such a discussion is out of order under this item.

As I said this afternoon, it seems to me that other hon. gentlemen are allowed a great deal of latitude, but I have to take the gun. My hon. friend opposite, the leader of the reconstruction party, has been longer in this house than I have; he knows the rules, and so do I, but when I speak I am 'he one who gets the gaff. I should like to know the reason why.
You are on the wrong side of the house.
If that is the reason, if I have to take the gaff, I shall take it.

The hon. gentleman
should move to the northeast corner.
The hon. gentleman will be lucky if he gets back into any corner after the next election.
My hon. friend should apply that statement to himself. I am safe enough; I shall be back.
The hon. member may be back in Ottawa but not in the house. I do not desire to depart from the rules of the house.
Hear, hear.

If that is a compliment, I accept it; if it is not, I reject it. I can quite understand giving money to the Canadian National Railways because that would be just taking it out of one pocket and putting it into another. It is Canadian money and it would be going back to the Canadian people, but as my hon. friend said-I was going to say my right hon. friend, and perhaps some day he will be-when you take a similar amount and hand it over to the Canadian Pacific Railway, they relieve themselves first and relieve the reliever afterwards. I can see many many ways in which that money could be better employed. As I say, this company wrote off nearly $3,500,000 as

depreciation on their steamships; they took that amount out of earnings and were still able to show a profit of $1,348,000. When they were asked why they did not declare a dividend they replied that they wanted some ready money. For what? It was not to be used in connection with anything in Canada; they wanted it in order to be ready to hand over to the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie Railway.
Order.

Order, quite true. Furthermore, we have to deal with the facts. If they are not dealt with here, they will be dealt with under some other subject. There is no sound reason why, to use the words of the leader of the reconstruction party, we should subsidize the Canadian Pacific Railway in the manner indicated. The Canadian Pacific Railway is a private corporation; let it look after itself. The company's own statement shows what they have. Their ships are practically new. The Empress of Britain is just new, the Duchess boats practically new, the "M" boats are not yet in their prime, and the Beaver boats, 10,000 ton freighters, are absolutely new.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must ask the hon. gentleman to observe the ruling of the chair.
I respect your ruling, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member must confine his remarks to the item under discussion. He is entirely out of order and I must ask him to observe the rules of the committee and see that his remarks bear entirely on the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have already given my ruling and the hon. member can appeal against it if he sees fit.

Since I have been in the parliament of Canada I have never taken exception to any ruling of the Speaker or of the Chairman and I do not propose to do so now. I accept the ruling and will confine my remarks strictly to the subject matter within the four corners of the item. But as we all pray before going to bed at night, if we pass away before morning, that He be merciful to us all as sinners; with the generosity of a Nova Scotian-and I see two of my Nova Scotia friends across the way-I leaveit at that.
The Minister of Railways referred to squandering, and I think that is true. I was trying to find the cause, and I think I see it in the reconstruction act which is now up in the red chamber. As I see it, at the end of the season so much is paid to the men employed; whatever is due is paid in a lump sum. and that is to help to carry them over
the winter. Now we all know that everybody has good intentions and we know the name of the place the way to which is paved with them, and the suggestion I have to offer is this, that the balance should be paid monthly or weekly and not in a lump sum. In a great many cases they might not intend it, but when the grey cold dawn of the morning after comes they will find they have nothing. They should be protected against themselves; their families should be protected. That is the only suggestion I make. If the balance due were distributed over the period of time during which the men might not be working, it would help their families. It might involve a little extra bookkeeping, but if it brought a little more happiness to the homes it might well be considered by the Minister of Railways. I know from my short acquaintance with him that his ability is outstanding and his kindness of heart is not excelled by any hon. gentleman's in this house. With that last word I shall not intrude again into the debate on this particular item.

Before this item is carried there is one matter to which I wish to refer. I have no objection to this item. When the Minister of Labour brought it in a few weeks ago as part of the government's scheme to close down the relief camps, I was heartily in favour of the proposal. I felt it was a good thing to try to liquidate these relief camps as soon as we possibly could. But as the Minister of Labour has said on several occasions during the past few weeks, we ought to take the long range view of this problem of unemployment, and I want to apply that principle for a moment or two to these particular items which are now before the committee. If I recall correctly what was stated to-night, the men are to be employed, not for six months as the minister has stated, but for four months in these camps. They will receive on an average approximately $275 each in the form of wages for four months' work in the camps; it may not be full time; it may be short time, but if the whole of the $3,100,000 were to be divided among ten thousand men it would be approximately $300 apiece. From that sum, however, must be deducted transportation, probably costs of construction of the camps, maybe one or two other items. Therefore I think, when it is all boiled down, the average amount of wages received will be in the neighbourhood of $275. Out of that sum the men will have to pay for, say four months' board. I do not know what that will amount to, but I have an idea that it will be about $1 a day. Add to that other expenses incidental to staying in one of those construction camps, and I venture

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
to assert that when the four months have gone the minimum expenditure of a man in the camps will have been about $175. In that event, when he leaves the camp he will probably have $100 at his disposal. At the time the camps close down the winter months will be upon us, and the first thing those young men will require will be a certain amount of winter clothing. When the individual has equipped himself in that respect he will be left with a comparatively small amount of money.
Now, taking that long range view which the Minister of Labour has suggested to the house and to this committee upon so many occasions during the past few weeks, I am wondering what will happen to these men who will be employed on construction work after they have left the camps with a small amount of money in their pockets. Has the government any considered policy based upon what may be expected to become of these men once they leave the camps? Do ministers suppose that if the men leave with $50, $75, or $100, that will be a solution of the unemployment question? That does not seem to me to be looking so very far ahead. We are now in the month of May. The men will soon be working in those construction camps if they are not doing so now. When September comes round they will have to leave those camps, and their natural course will be to drift to the larger industrial centres. In September or October very few will be available for any farm work, assuming that farm work can be found for them. Has the Minister of Railways or the Minister of Labour any plans in mind or any suggestions to make as to what will be the policy of the government once these relief works close down? In asking this question I am merely adopting that long range view of the situation which the minister himself urged should be taken.

I should like
again to call attention to paragraph (d). As I understand the explanations made by the two ministers in discussing the bill, the agreement is intended by the government in the first instance to take care of single men from these relief camps, and if there are 10,000 of them they will be used for that purpose. The Minister of Labour said that there was nothing in the bill to prevent the government from using other unemployed if it should turn out that there were not 10,000 men available from the relief camps for this purpose. In view of their effort to close the camps there is a certain amount of justification, so far as the government is concerned, for this item in the estimates, but paragraph (d), it seems to me,

should not be there. I do not think that, as has been explained by the two ministers, any part of this money should be used for anything but the payment of labour, wages to the relief camp men if they are available, or to others if there are not enough men from the relief camps. Why should the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National Railways be paid for materials that are not used? Those materials will not be lost; they will be needed for other purposes. The expenditures made upon them by the railways will not be wasted if 10,000 men are not provided by the government; and on the minister's own explanation paragraph (d) should not be there. The purpose of this is to give work. All the money provided by the government should be used to pay wages. The railways should be perfectly willing to supply all the materials, and if by chance some of them should not be used this year they can be sold or used next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is what the lawyers call a saving clause. The Department of Justice has put-
Saving the railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No, it is a saving to this government. The department has to be very careful that it does not get the government into difficulties. Without that clause we might be agreeing to supply the railways 10,000 men, and in this free country it might be difficult to do that. We have no power to order these men as we like. If my right hon. friend will look closely at this paragraph he will see that it provides for this payment only in the event of our not fulfilling our agreement to furnish
10,000	men, and if we ask the railways to make elaborate preparations to receive men who are not supplied, we simply compensate them for expenditures they made, due to our fault or failure to furnish men. Common sense assures us that we shall be able to furnish a substantial number of men and there will be no such costs involved .to the railways as this paragraph contemplates.

If there are not
sufficient men from the relief camps, are the government prepared to take other unemployed? They know 10,000 men can be provided, and I do not understand the object of this paragraph. If the Canadian Pacific buy ties which cannot be used this year because sufficient men are not supplied by the government, the ties are there, and they are worth the money; why should the government pay for them?

Supply-Railways-Relief Works

I should like ho ask the minister whether there is any doubt that other labour will be employed provided sufficient men cannot ibe obtained from the oamps. It seems to me there should be no doubt at all on that point. In every city in this country we have a large number of men who are not on relief owing only to the fact that they have such a pride that they would rather almost starve to death to keep off, and for their pride or .patriotism they are being penalized under this legislation. To me that is the worst feature of it. Men who are not quite so patriotic, who more willingly went into the camps-and I know many of them are there against their will-are to be the first to get help, while these others, many of whom I know personally, who Struggled to keep out of the camps, are not going to get employment under this provision. I would like to have assurance from the minister that if there is any chance of the number of unemployed men in the camps not being sufficient to supply the number required on the railways, these other men of whom I speak will be employed. I recognize that the purpose of the government is to do away with the unemployment camps, and that is the reason for taking these men first. I think we all agree with that, but I want to be assured that these other men of whom I have spoken will have an opportunity of employment. All the more should that be done because it appears that if we are not able to supply the
10,000	men we must give the companies the money which they are supposed to be out of pocket in preparing for the work to be done. I say "supposed to be" because I feel that there is not going to be very much preparation in advance for this work except such as will -be useful later on. So if I can have from the minister the assurance that these men will be given work I shall be much better satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I should be very glad indeed if it turned out that the government was unable to find ten thousand men in the camps for this work, a contingency which is contemplated in paragraph (d). Only a lawyer versed in technicalities would think of that, but I understand how a man who desired to ensure the protection of the government would foresee it. But I think I can assure my hon. friend that there will be no such difficulty.
My point is that if they are not in the camps-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They will be furnished in some way.

My colleague has raised a question which has not been answered, and which I think should be answered. We are to some extent handicapped in this committee on account of the way in which the votes are divided up. On an earlier estimate we asked a question of the Minister of Labour and he said that he could not answer because certain matters came under other departments. Now we have come to one of these other departments, the Department of Railways and Canals, and although we are dealing with the estimates of that department I take it that we are in reality dealing with the question of unemployment. The only reason we have an estimate of this kind is that of unemployment. Now for some days we have been discussing the general question, how to deal with the large numbers of unemployed men. Apparently the scheme for dealing with the men now in the camps is to put 10,000 of them to work on the railways and hope that the remainder will go on farms. We are dealing now with the provision for the 10,000. I think the minister who is in charge of this estimate cannot avoid looking at the larger question of unemployment, with which the item is supposed to deal. I need not go over the ground covered by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps). This estimate, as he points out, makes provision for the men for a few months. They work; they get wages; that is an improvement on the old camp arrangement. But remember that the railways, including the Canadian Pacific, a privately owned road, get the dole. The railways get relief, their portion of the $3,100,000. And they take no chances whatever, they are protected fully, even against the possibility of loss. The men are employed for the time they can be used; they give something in return for their wages; they give something in return to the public road in one ease and in the other to the private corporation. Now, what is going to happen when they have done this four months' work? There is adequate provision that the railways may suffer no loss, but have we any way of providing for the men at the end of the four months? What does the government propose to do? Are these men to be turned out when the winter comes, as the contractors in the west used to turn out the horses, to forage for themselves? In that case, with the dismantling of the camps, the situation will be worse than ever. I think my colleague is quite within his rights in asking a question which relates to an essential feature in the whole scheme,

Supply-Railways-Relief Works
whether any provision is to be made for the men at the conclusion of the four or five months' work. That is a reasonable question on which we should have some information from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is scarcely possible for a minister or anyone else to chart the future course of 10,000 individual men. The difficulty of the men in the camps-they have expressed it frequently in the public press and otherwise-is that in the camps their prospect is hopeless. They have no opportunity of securing employment and they receive no money. Now we are finding them employment; surely that is the first step towards rehabilitation. A great deal of concern has been shown here as to why these men should be picked out for this preferment as against other men. At any rate they are being provided with work, ordinary work that ordinary men can perform and live by. My hon. friend lives in a country where employment is seasonal and he knows that a great many men never do anything but this seasonal work, and in spite of that some of them raise families; yet these are all single men. I am confident that these men are similar to other men, who follow seasonal work and are never sure of employment for longer than a four or five month period, because construction work is always seasonal. I know that many men have done well in that class of work. We are starting these men in such work. Some may fail. My hon. friend is acquainted with the machinery for looking after the unemployed in this country; they are not going to be allowed to starve. We are placing these men's feet on the ladder of employment; we believe they will do as other men following the construction industries; when one project is completed they will find other employment. In other words we are establishing these men in employment for a period at least.
Then the minister has no plan for continuing employment for the four months?
Have you?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Has my hon. friend?

No, we have not power, but this government went into power on the express understanding that they were to deal with this matter. Apparently they are dealing with it by exactly the same methods as employed by the late government, except they are trying to do it on a little cheaper scale. If anyone is to be helped by this arrangement is is the railways.
And the men.

The railways are being protected against any possible risk. It is all very well to say that these men are having their feet set on the ladder, but are we going to kick away the ladder just when it is set up? Does the minister really believe that in four months, at the rate of pay proposed, these men can save enough to see them through the winter? I do not think he can really believe that. With the whole unemployment situation as it is

and a lot of us know about seasonal unemployment in the west-what are these men going to do when October comes, with no provision whatever made? Surely, if this is the government's plan, or an important part of their plan to deal with unemployment, they ought to be able to see things through a little further than four months.

I should like to ask the
Minister of Railways a question. No doubt he believes in equity, yet I find the amount of money being paid the Canadian Pacific Railway is the same as is being paid to the Canadian National Railways, although the latter named system has a mileage of 24,000 as against only 17,000 miles of the former. Therefore there is a difference of 7,000 miles. Why should not these moneys be apportioned according to mileage, so that each railway would get its fair share, and the Canadian Pacific Railway would not get the unearned increment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Amount to be applied by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada towards the cost of actual construction work for the protection, safety, and convenience of the public in respect of highway grade crossings of railways, as the governor in council may from time to time determine, $1,000,000.

Has the minister any particular schemes in view for the expenditure of this money, or will he simply pass it on to the board of railway commissioners? As I remember it, the Minister of Railways recommends the points at which this work is to be done. Is that the procedure?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My understanding is that application may be made by any one to the board of railway commissioners.
Directly?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, either by the railways
or by persons. The board of railway commissioners examine the situation, and if they

Supply-Railway Commission
approve the work they make application to the Department of Railways and Canals for the expenditure. The million dollar fund will be administered entirely by the board of railway commissioners.

The Minister of
Railways has to give his approval before any of these schemes is put into effect, does he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Recommendation is made to
council by the Minister of Railways.

The board of railway commissioners consider the application. If the minister receives one in the first instance he passes it on to the board; it is considered by them; inspection is made on the spot, and if they think the work may be done properly under this vote the recommendation will come back to the minister who has it in his power or discretion either to ask for an order in council approving, or to let the matter drop.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I assume that is correct,
although as a matter of fact, if a recommendation is made by the board, it is passed on automatically.
The minister has discretion which is not often used; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

Before the item is carried there are one or two figures I should like to lay before the minister. I do this in an endeavour to show where we are drifting in connection with money spent in the elimination of crossings. I do not know whether hon. members are aware that in the past twenty years, out of a total of 31,784 crossings only 1,252 have been protected, leaving 30,532 unprotected crossings. In that time the total amount of money spent in Canada on crossings has been $36,000,000. My reason for presenting these figures to the minister is that I am endeavouring to point- out where we are drifting, and I am asking if we are spending the money to the best advantage. A few years back the system was changed by the railway companies, at which time they displaced workmen by eliminating the watchmen and taking away barriers, instituting a new system known as the wigwag signal. May I point out to the minister that the installation of the new system costs about $5,000. an amount equal to a watchman's pay for eight or ten years. The strange point is that the change has not protected the lives of the people, at all. As a matter of fact deaths and accidents have increased since
the elimination of the watchmen and barriers and the installation of the so-called new system. I for one would like to know who receives the royalty on these installations, and possibly the minister could find out why the Canadian National Railways are charged more than the Canadian Pacific Railway for the installation. This is a serious matter. It is true that a bill has been introduced by a private member. I do not know whether it will bring about the desired result, but I know that after looking through the report of the board of railway commissioners I have come to the conclusion that never in the lifetime of any member of this house, nor in the time of any generation yet born will we eliminate railway crossings in Canada if we proceed at our present rate, unless we pull up the tracks.
The information in the publication by the board of railway commissioners shows that crossings are increasing rather than decreasing and yet we have spent only $36,000,000 in twenty-five years, and are spending only $1,000,000 at this time. We are satisfied with saying: Oh well, by spending a million dollars we are doing something to protect life and limb at railway crossings. The matter has only been scratched. I listened attentively to the observations of the hon. member for East Kootenay when he stated that $5,000,000 would not be sufficient to eliminate the great number of unprotected crossings. We must protect those crossings, if we are going to do the job properly. I would ask the minister to investigate the matter carefully. I believe we would do well to replace the barriers on our highways. It is true that most provinces have regulations stipulating that buses must stop at crossings, but I do not believe we will ever pass laws compelling every motor car to stop before attempting to cross. We may do that, but I have my doubts.
It is my view that the whole matter should be given careful consideration. When one considers the number of accidents which have taken place he is at once aware of the serious nature of the problem. In 1935 there were 242 accidents, in which 114 persons were killed and 304 injured. That is not a complete total of the injured people, because all the figures are not given by the board; only serious accidents and deaths are reported to them. If one examines the figures available for the period between 1915 and 1932 he will find that crossings protected by gates showed a death ratio of fourteen per thousand as against thirty-eight per thousand protected by the modern method.
As I have pointed out, crossings are increasing in number, and deaths are increasing. Yet
Supply-Railway Commission

we are spending these large sums of money. I know the minister is anxious to have the item passed, and I shall not hold- it up, but I thought it was my duty at least to show him that the matter is far more serious than has been hitherto indicated.
Do I understand that none of this money will be used for the elimination of level crossings?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The whole sum will be used for that purpose. The board of railway commissioners will have the disposition of it, and I understand practically all of it will be for the elimination of level crossings.

I am familiar with crossings along trunk roads in Ontario, and I know that those crossings have -been death traps for years. It is indicated in the vote that "the governor in council -may from time to time determine." He is baking a -mighty long time to arrive at his determination. I agree with the hon. -members for Kootenay East and New Westminster in their statement that the amount should be augmented ten or fifteen times. We should speed u-p the work of removing level crossings and death traps in Canada.

May I add a word to my earlier observations. It must be obvious to hon. members that this vote does not represent a serious attempt to face the question of the elimination of level crossings. In the first place it is applicable only to places where applications are made and where local authorities are prepared to shoulder their share of the cost. The minister will correct me if I am wrong when I state that under the law the municipality, or the applicant, must pay one-third, the railway must pay one-third and the balance comes out of this provision. Some division of that kind is made, I believe. I may not be quite correct, but there is a division. It is obvious that it will be only certain municipalities or cities that will make application. As the hon. member said a moment ago there are within fifty miles of this city crossings that anyone who drives a motor knows to be veritable death traps, but the local municipality is either unwilling or unable to make application with respect to them, and so the death trap continues to exist. There is no impelling force to induce any authority to take hold of the situation, and so it just stays as it is, and that is all there is to it.
This is a great national problem. Canada ought to be ashamed of its highways in relation to grade crossings. My hon. friend said that $36,000,000 has been spent in twent-y-
five years, but he must remember that those tremendously expensive crossings in Montreal and at the station in Toronto come under this grade separation fund, and I imagine that the major portion of that $36,000,000 has been used in the great cities, which does not touch at all the situation we have described as it exists throughout the country. I am sonry that the minister and the government seem to resent suggestions of this kind. It is a vital matter. In the first place there is a tremendous need for employment, and this is a case where provision can be made not only for employment but for the elimination of one of the greatest outstanding, shall I say, national dangers.
When I said $5,000,000 I -think I put the arnount very low. I would suggest that the minister and the government consider increasing this expenditure by an additional sum, though perhaps not in this estimate, because I know a great many members of this house are very much in earnest about this particular problem. Members, particularly those supporting the government, do not like to embarrass it, but I want to say to the minister and the government that these are constructive and useful suggestions which catch the ear of the people of this country who understand the situation, and they are willing to support any government which will take the necessary measures. It is not a political question ; it is not a question affecting a-ny section ; it is a national question. This is a great opportunity to meet a great national need.
I urge upon the minister once again to consider a definite policy apart altogether from the present statute, which, although it may operate all right in normal times, is restrictive, and seriously to consider a forward movement and the establishment of a national policy in this matter.

I speak as a prejudiced
witness, which I admit very frankly, in view of the fact that there are in my riding, which is the municipal riding of the east part of Toronto, three grade crossings, not only exceedingly dangerous -but also very important from the point of view of the amount of traffic that is compelled to pass over them. For many years the question has been discussed and rediscussed of the possibility of changing these grade crossings into subways or otherwise, and if my hon. friend from Broadview (Mr. Church) and my hon. friend from Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) were here they w-ould bear me out in what I have to say.
I would ask the minister if this vote that we are asked to pass to-night may be regarded

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
as simply the first vote along the lines suggested to him by those who have spoken during the last few minutes. One could say a great deal under this item on the necessity of such work as is here contemplated being done on a wide national scale, and I earnestly urge upon the minister that not only in municipalities but throughout the country, on the highways and byways, there is much work of this kind that needs to be done in the interests not only of safety but of subdividing traffic, which is something very much to be desired. I would ask the minister if this may be regarded as simply the first vote along these lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This vote is supplementary
to the ordinary grade crossing vote, which as we all know is a statutory grant towards the removal of grade crossings. This, in the opinion of the railway commissioners, will cover the government's share of the applications which are made to the board and of which the board approves. If more money is needed I think the government will be glad to consider a larger grant next year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
To provide for repairs and improvements to the canals, harbours, and elevators maintained and operated by the Department of Railways and Canals, $167,600.
This seems to be quite in order, but why should this item not appear in the ordinary estimates? Why is it in the special supplementaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This amount is for work that could be done this year or could be deferred. While the work is necessary, it is not necessary in the immediate year. The item has been put in because the work covers a series of small projects that will employ considerable labour rather widely distributed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Deficit of Canadian National Railway Company
